cleanIntro: Smith & Wesson covers the Model 66 in its manual for modern-style J, K, L and N frame revolvers, and that book publishes no disassembly at all. Cleaning is done with the revolver whole and the cylinder swung out, and everything below carries the manual's own words and the page they sit on.

steps.title: Make sure this is the book for your revolver
steps.action: This procedure comes from Smith & Wesson's manual for modern-style J, K, L and N frame revolvers, and the Model 66 is a K-frame. Smith & Wesson publishes separate manuals for two revolvers it does not cover here — the BODYGUARD 38 and the X-FRAME 460 and 500 Magnum — so satisfy yourself you are not holding one of those. The model number and the internal serial number are stamped inside the yoke and can only be read with the cylinder swung open.
steps.prose: The book never prints "Model 66" anywhere in it. It scopes itself by FRAME rather than by model number, which is why it can cover several decades of K-frame production in one document, Performance Center guns included. Read the number in the yoke before you accept that this is your revolver's manual, because that is the only place your gun states which model it is.
steps.quote: There are separate manuals for S&W® BODYGUARD® 38 and X-FRAME 460 & 500 Magnum revolvers - available free upon request or via download from our web site.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL

steps.title: Thumbpiece forward, cylinder out to the left
steps.action: With your finger off the trigger and outside the trigger guard and the muzzle in a safe direction, press the thumbpiece fully forward and hold it there, then push the cylinder out to the left. Check that every charge hole is free of live ammunition and that the bore is clear of obstructions.
steps.prose: Hold the thumbpiece forward through the whole swing rather than tapping it — release it early and the cylinder stop drags in its notch and the cylinder binds halfway out. Charge holes and bore are two separate checks and the manual asks for both: a clear cylinder tells you nothing about what is sitting in the barrel.
steps.quote: You must verify that all charge holes (chambers) are free of live ammunition and that the bore is free of obstructions.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Inspecting Your Revolver, p.15
steps.warn: Always ensure the firearm is unloaded before inspecting, disassembling, assembling or cleaning, and always keep the muzzle pointed in a safe direction.

steps.title: Muzzle up, extractor rod through, then count
steps.action: Hold the cylinder out, point the barrel upward in a safe direction and press the extractor rod through the cylinder so everything lifts clear. Take the rounds or cases out of the gun and count them against the charge holes in your cylinder.
steps.prose: Muzzle up is the whole trick: with the barrel down, a case that only lifts partway slides straight back into its hole and reads as an empty chamber from the front. Let the rod return under its own spring afterwards, and if it drags, fouling behind the ratchet is what is doing it.
steps.caution: Carefully count the cartridges or spent casings to be sure that you have recovered all of them.
steps.quote: With the barrel pointing upward in a safe direction, press the extractor rod through the cylinder and remove all cartridges or casings from the cylinder
steps.cite:

steps.title: Read the barrel: .357 Mag, and what else it may fire
steps.action: The cartridge designation is rolled on the barrel of this revolver and that marking is the instruction. Smith & Wesson's alternate-ammunition table on page 9 lists one substitution against the marking your .357 Mag barrel carries: 38 S&W Special and 38 S&W Special +P. Nothing outside the marking and that line belongs in the cylinder.
steps.prose: The substitution runs one way only. A .357 Mag chamber will take the shorter cartridge on that list quite happily; the shorter gun will not take this one, and a round that is too long or too hot can still start into a chamber it does not belong in. Firing the shorter round leaves a hard carbon ring at the front of each charge hole, which is why the cleaning below asks for the full length of every chamber.
steps.quote: Locate the cartridge designation marked on the firearm. This information indicates the correct ammunition that must be used in this firearm.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Ammunition, p.9
steps.warn: IN SOME CASES, A ROUND OF AMMUNITION NOT SPECIFIED ON YOUR FIREARM AND NOT LISTED AS ALTERNATE AMMUNITION IN THIS MANUAL, MAY FIT INTO THE CHAMBER.

steps.title: Nothing marked +P+, and nothing reloaded
steps.action: Ammunition marked +P+ must not be used in Smith & Wesson firearms. Plain +P is a different case: it generates higher pressures than standard ammunition, which may affect wear and may mean the revolver needs service more often. Reloaded or handloaded ammunition that has not been pressure-tested does not go in this gun either.
steps.prose: The objection to +P+ is not that it is hot, it is that the marking names no defined pressure limit at all, so two boxes wearing it can be a long way apart in what they actually generate. If cases have started extracting hard, the manual has a specific answer before you change anything: clean the charge holes thoroughly with solvent, and if it persists, change brands.
steps.caution: Never use non-standard, damaged, corroded or reloaded, (handloaded) ammunition which has not been subjected to internal ballistic pressure testing.
steps.quote: “Plus-P-Plus” (+P+) ammunition must not be used in Smith & Wesson firearms.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL

steps.title: The barrel is not yours to remove
steps.action: Leave the barrel alone. On a revolver built with a barrel and barrel-shroud, the stainless steel barrel tube comes out only in a qualified gunsmith's hands with a special tool from Smith & Wesson, and it goes back in with that same tool and an accurate torque wrench.
steps.prose: This sits under a heading that reads FOR USE BY TRAINED GUNSMITHS ONLY, and the reason is structural rather than cautious: the shroud is keyed into the frame by a metal tab, so a standard barrel wrench twists the shroud against that tab and can take the frame with it. Nothing in routine cleaning needs the barrel off.
steps.quote: The stainless steel barrel tube must only be removed by a qualified gunsmith using a special tool available from Smith & Wesson. The barrel assembly is re-installed using the same tool and an accurate torque wrench.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Gunsmith Advisory, p.26

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: An open, empty cylinder is the whole of it. Smith & Wesson publishes no disassembly procedure for this revolver — the cylinder, yoke, extractor, hammer and lockwork all stay in the frame, and the sideplate stays on. Everything the cleaning below asks for is reachable through that open window.
steps.prose: Read the manual's own boundary carefully, because it is unusual: the caution points you at "the Field Stripping and Inspection sections of this manual", and this book has an Inspection section and no Field Stripping section at all. For a revolver that is not an omission, it is the answer — there is nothing to strip.
steps.quote: Never disassemble your firearm beyond the instructions in the Field Stripping and Inspection sections of this manual.
steps.cite:

deepAbsentReason: The J/K/L/N revolver manual documents inspecting, loading, firing, decocking, unloading, sight adjustment, moon-clip use, cleaning, maintenance and storage — and no disassembly procedure of any kind. Its table of contents has no field-stripping section, and the only teardown it names, removal of the barrel tube, it assigns to a qualified gunsmith with a factory tool and a torque wrench. Searched and re-confirmed against the cached document on 2026-08-20: Smith & Wesson publishes no deeper procedure for the Model 66. Basic clean as set out above covers routine care; anything past an open cylinder is gunsmith territory. Note the manual's own p.30 caution refers the reader to "the Field Stripping and Inspection sections of this manual" and no field-stripping section exists in it.

cleaning.name: BORE AND CHARGE HOLES
tasks: Remove excessive firing residue from the bore and every charge hole with a properly fitted brass brush dipped in gun cleaning solvent
Finish each one with a dry cotton cloth patch to carry the residue and solvent back out
Clean the FULL length of every charge hole — firing the shorter 38 S&W Special in a .357 Mag chamber leaves a hard ring partway down that will stop a full-length round seating
If cases have been extracting hard, clean the charge holes thoroughly with solvent before you conclude anything about the ammunition

cleaning.name: CYLINDER FACE, EXTRACTOR AND FRAME WINDOW
tasks: Clean the front face of the cylinder and the rear face of the barrel — that is where the flash ring builds and where a barrel/cylinder gap starts to close up
Clean the rear face of the cylinder and the extractor star, then press the extractor rod out and clean behind the star
Wipe out the frame window and the recoil shield; grit behind the star is the usual reason a cylinder will not close cleanly

cleaning.name: EXTERIOR, LUBRICATION AND STORAGE
tasks: Clean the exterior with a non-abrasive cloth and take off every trace of cleaning solution, oil and fingerprints — finger moisture left on steel starts a corrosion process
Avoid prolonged solvent immersion and prolonged ultrasonic cleaning; never use ammoniated or other strong alkaline solvents on a Smith & Wesson
After cleaning, lightly coat the metal parts inside and out with a high quality gun oil
In a cold climate pick an oil weight that will not congeal and slow the action

For long storage oil the bore, chambers and internal mechanism and coat the external mechanism and barrel with an anti-rust oil; do not store the revolver in leather or heavy cloth, and never with a plug in the barrel
Check for signs of wear every time you clean it, and if wear is noted, stop using the revolver

reassembly: Nothing came off the revolver, so there is nothing to rebuild — push the cylinder into the frame until the thumbpiece moves forward and latches. Press it home rather than swinging or flicking it shut.
Rotate the closed cylinder by hand until the bolt drops into a notch, so you know it is locked and indexed.
Dry-patch the bore and every charge hole before the revolver is carried or fired again; oil left in a chamber raises pressure and drives the case back against the recoil shield.
fncheck: With every charge hole confirmed empty and the bore clear, close the cylinder and check that it latches and that the thumbpiece releases it cleanly. Pointed in a safe direction, cycle the action double action and confirm the cylinder indexes and locks at every stop and that the trigger returns fully forward between shots. If your revolver has an exposed or shrouded hammer, cock it and check the single action notch holds and that the hammer decocks under thumb control back to its at-rest forward position rather than stopping partway.
